title: Layered architectures and the medallion model
summary: Why data platforms are organised in layers, how classic EDW, medallion and dbt layering map onto each other, and what contracts hold between layers.

blocks.text: Almost every data platform, whatever its vendor, organises data into a sequence of layers from raw to consumable. The names change (staging, ODS, bronze, raw, landing; integration, silver, conformed; presentation, gold, marts) but the reasons are the same. Part III covers each layer in depth; this chapter explains why they exist and how to keep them from multiplying.

items: **Separation of concerns**: landing data reliably, making it correct, and making it useful are different problems with different owners, test strategies and change rates.
**Replayability**: if the raw layer is kept unchanged, any downstream bug can be fixed and the result rebuilt without asking the source again. Sources often cannot resend history.
**Blast radius**: a change in a source schema should break one staging model, not fifty dashboards.
**Reuse**: cleaning and conforming done once in the middle layer is shared by every mart instead of repeated per report.
**Access control**: raw data often contains PII and secrets; consumers get the curated layers only (chapter 34).

blocks.text: The medallion naming was popularised by Databricks for lakehouses; dbt's staging/intermediate/marts convention comes from dbt Labs' project-structure guide. Neither invented layering. A useful mental model: bronze is **what the source said**, silver is **what is true about the business entities**, gold is **what a consumer needs to answer questions**.

blocks.text: Medallion is a set of quality levels, not a physical rule. Bronze, silver and gold can be schemas in one Snowflake database, namespaces in one Iceberg catalog, or separate storage accounts. What matters is that each layer has a clear contract and owner.
A layer is only useful if the next layer can rely on it. Write down what each layer guarantees, and test those guarantees at the boundary (chapter 33).

head: Boundary
Producer guarantees
Typical checks
rows: Every delivered record lands exactly once per load, with ingestion metadata
Row counts vs source, file manifests, no parse failures silently dropped
Typed columns, one row per entity key (or per version), conformed keys and codes
Unique and not-null keys, accepted values, referential integrity, freshness
Declared grain, documented measures, stable names, freshness SLA
Grain uniqueness, reconciliation to finance totals, metric tests

blocks.text: dbt model contracts (`contract: {enforced: true}`) check column names and types at build time; schema tests check content. In Spark and Iceberg pipelines the same idea is implemented with expectation libraries or custom assertions in the job. The mechanism matters less than the rule: no layer consumes another layer's internals.

Skipping layers is the usual decay: a dashboard reads bronze directly because silver is late, then a second one copies it. Within a year, the same parsing logic exists in five places with five bugs. If consumers need something faster, make the proper path faster.
12.4 How many layers is too many?
Every layer costs storage, compute, latency and, most of all, cognitive load: a column traced through seven layers takes an engineer an afternoon to debug. Common inflation patterns:

items: *Platinum*, *diamond* or *bronze-plus* layers added to fix a problem that belonged inside an existing layer.
One physical layer per transformation step, when most steps could be CTEs or views inside one model.
Separate *pre-silver* and *post-silver* layers per team because ownership was never agreed.
Materialising every intermediate model as a table instead of views or ephemeral models.

blocks.text: A good default is three **logical** layers (raw, conformed, serving) plus the semantic layer on top. Inside a layer you may have several model stages (dbt staging and intermediate both live within the bronze-to-silver range), but they should not each get a new name, owner and access policy. Add a layer only when it has a different contract, owner or access policy than its neighbours.

blocks.text: Layers are often blamed for latency: if each hop runs every hour, gold is up to three hours stale. That is a scheduling problem, not a layering one. Options: trigger downstream models on upstream completion instead of on fixed schedules (chapter 30), process layers incrementally (chapter 14), or run continuous pipelines where each layer is a streaming job or a dynamic table with a target lag (chapter 27). A bronze-silver-gold pipeline with minute-level latency is entirely feasible.

blocks.title: Consolidating a sprawling warehouse
blocks.text: An insurer's warehouse had grown to schemas named raw, landing, stage, ods, core, core2, conformed, mart and report, with no documented rules. The platform team mapped every schema to bronze, silver or gold by its actual contract, merged five schemas, and enforced in CI that models could only reference their own layer or the one below.
items: Model count dropped by about a third once duplicate cleaning logic was removed
Lineage became readable in the catalog
Access policies shrank to three role grants, one per layer

blocks.text: A two-sided marketplace ingests its Postgres database via CDC, payment events from a payment provider's webhooks, and ad spend from three marketing APIs. Define the layers you would create, the contract at each boundary, who owns each layer, and the one place you would allow an exception for latency.
hints: Which data is replayable from the source and which is not?
Where do payment events and orders get conformed to the same order key?

items: Layers exist for replayability, separation of concerns, reuse, blast-radius control and access control.
EDW staging/integration/presentation, medallion bronze/silver/gold and dbt staging/intermediate/marts describe the same progression.
Each boundary needs a written, tested contract; no layer reads another layer's internals.
Three logical layers plus a semantic layer is a strong default; add one only for a new contract, owner or policy.
Latency problems are solved with incremental and event-driven processing, not by skipping layers.

blocks.q: What is the strongest reason to keep the raw layer unchanged?
options: Downstream bugs can be fixed and rebuilt without asking sources to resend data
It removes the need for data quality tests
It is cheaper to store than curated data
blocks.explain: Replayability is the key benefit; many sources cannot resend history. Raw is not faster for BI and does not replace tests.

blocks.q: In a dbt project on a medallion platform, which models implement the silver layer?
blocks.explain: Staging models type and rename per source and intermediate models join, deduplicate and conform; together they produce silver. Sources point at bronze, marts are gold.

blocks.q: When is adding a new layer justified?
options: Whenever a new transformation step is added
When a team wants its own schema
When it has a different contract, owner or access policy from its neighbours
blocks.explain: A layer should mark a real boundary. Transformation steps belong inside a layer as models or CTEs; slow queries need layout or materialisation fixes.

blocks.q: Gold is three hours stale because each of three layers runs hourly. What is the best fix?
options: Run every layer every minute with full refreshes
Trigger downstream layers on upstream completion and process incrementally
blocks.explain: The staleness comes from independent schedules. Event-driven triggering plus incremental processing removes the stacked delay without losing layers; full refreshes every minute would be very expensive.
